text_fidelity_a:
SleepPhones AcousticSheep Classic | Corded Headphones for Sleep, Travel, and More | The Original and Most Comfortable Headphones for Sleeping | Soft Gray - Fleece Fabric (Size M) I fall asleep to audiobooks, and have tried a lot of speakers and headphones with mixed results. My husband bought me these AcousticSheep SleepPhones recently, and what a difference they make! They're very comfortable - okay, the mediums are a little large for me, but I've found a way to position them so they work perfectly. The speakers are thin and pliable, so they're comfortable even if you roll over and lie on them, and the sound is pleasant - not too boomy or too shrill, and you can move the headband so you can listen in both ears or only one, if you prefer.

The one catch is that the wires leading out of the headphones are pretty thin, and judging my previous experience using many headsets and speakers in bed, they're going to break inside at some point. Then I'll either have to order more or perhaps do a little creative wire work and attach new, stronger wires. I'd be perfectly happy to replace these once a year as they've improved my quality of sleep (I'm used to waking when I roll onto a hard plastic speaker or earphone).

BTW, the headband itself is sooo soft and comfy - none of the headbands I've used on my hair over the years are this cozy.

Like it said on the package, these truly are pajamas for your ears ;-)

***Update Feb 9, 2014***

It's been just short of a year since I write the above review. Since then, I ordered a second smaller pair of SleepPhones, the band of which wasn't as soft and furry, but it was good for wearing when doing housework. This one didn't come in the same packaging - the packaging was more minimual. My original pair of SleepPhones' wire on the left ear did indeed break, and I bought a third pair. This was in a much smaller package, but was furry and comfy as the first set. Hopefully it will last a bit longer than my original pair - the wires are a bit more robust.
text_fidelity_b: SleepPhones AcousticSheep Classic | Corded Headphones for Sleep, Travel, and More | The Original and Most Comfortable Headphones for Sleeping | Soft Gray - Fleece Fabric (Size M)

text_fidelity_a: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White This was purchased as a gift. I, the writer of this review, am the recipient of the gift. After about a year of "monkeying around" with this piece of technology, I have unplugged it and relegated it to a drawer. It simply doesn't work consistently. It often " has trouble connecting to the internet", even though nothing has changed. It often gets the voice commands wrong, or just doesn't respond. When it is working, (we use it mostly to stream music to a sound bar that I bought just to use with the dot by Blue tooth connection), it will often just quit, or pause and restart. I have had several conversations with the help desk at Amazon, and although very pleasant, the solution always seems to be the same. Turn it off and reinstall it. Not doing that any more. The WiFi is one room away, and lap tops, tablets and smart phones all work just fine in this room and others through out the house. It is sad, because this seemed like a great solution to get some music into this room without blasting it from several rooms away, but alas, it is a bust. Some of the things that it did, like the "this day in history" were fun, or the jokes she would tell were so silly that they were just funny, but that doesn't make the Dot worth the time, effort, or money. Save your money and buy a Blue tooth speaker for your phone. You'll be glad you did.
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

text_fidelity_a:
Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count After 40-some years on the technical side of electrochemical fabrication (12" wafer fab) and manufacturing that included the IBM PS1 & PS2 birth … cleanliness is Godliness. I've likely tried every chemical variant of cleaner ever invented, though many fewer are now permitted for USA use.

Though impractical for the laptop, some excellent cleaners in the $1000/gal category might be suggested for cleansing strategic missile-related monitors and surfaces. The value and reliability of what device you are cleaning is the most critical consideration when choosing a cleaner. A wrong choice might pay back immediately with bad results, dissolving the anti-reflective coating or lamination of the touch screen overlay, removing specialized keyboard paints, ruining distinctive finishes, etc. For another, that same choice might do a bang-up job on the big screen at home, but when used on a laptop, it slowly dissolves and/or corrodes critical interconnects as you pass through dewpoints on that 17-hour airplane ride to Sydney.

Q: What is the best cleaner to shine on my $1500 laptop?

A: Not the cheapest $4/qt cleaner. Not one of grandma's window elixirs.

Behind the scenes, there is likely no other technical discussion as critical as cleaning and cleaners. Billions are spent every year on the problem. What I know from experience is that an alcohol solvent-based cleaner does a pretty good job erasing the symbology that makes my lighted keyboard legible. I look for a cleaner to remove the latent crusty-goo residue left by that anti-viral covid computer cleaner six months ago. Some cleaners with notionally benign saponifiers that sell under the enviro-friendly, "Green!", "non-GMO!" moniker is known to corrode solder joints and electro-plating to short the keyboard and LCD/OLED out.

Finding the right balance between solvent and saponifiers has not evolved smoothly. Saponifiers remove organics. The stuff that sprays out of your mouth and nose when yelling at the laptop. Solvents remove inorganics like hand cream, french fry grease, and Cheeto dust. I've rolled up all of this wisdom in my 'Rule #446 - Do not buy the cheapest electronics cleaner. Ever.'

This Monster cleaner is not cheap. It's a premium cleaner under a known premium brand. Given Monster brands, cleaning processes are the #1 priority for their established long-lived high-fidelity interconnection. My laptop has a touch screen that demands a non-delaminating cleaner and a lighted keyboard with that funky paint and laser-etched symbology. This Monster cleaner did an unexpectedly quick, no-smudge job on the laptop. All is good.
text_fidelity_b: Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count

text_fidelity_a:
Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO V2 CPU Air Cooler with SickleFlow 120, PWM Fan, Direct Contact Technology, 4 Copper Heat Pipes for AMD Ryzen/Intel LGA1700/1200/1151, Silver/Black I have had this CPU fan now going on 5 months. I love this fan. I hadn't upgraded for nearly 10 years and decided on an AMD FM2 Black Edition 6300 6-core CPU with an MSI 970A-G43 Plus economy Micro Board and 16GB of Corsair Memory 4GBx4 in the 4 slots. I use my computer for gaming and all around use. I wanted a CPU cooler that would be quiet and still keep my cpu cool when I cranked it up for high-performance gaming. I found it with this AND it didn't break the bank. With the Turbo Clock OC setting it will idle down and bolt up to 4300mhz seamlessly while the fan moves from it's WHISPER silent 36c idle and general use, to it's 42c full bore o'clocked gaming use. The fan keeps it cool, and never does the fan become obtrusive or loud.

This fan is BIG. Don't even consider it if you have a micro or small mid-tower case. Your case must be generous in it's width to accommodate this cooler. Be sure to check the dimensions of your case with the unit. I have an older Antec 900 case it fit snugly into. I did have to remove the optional side window cooler intake fan I had installed with the prev board, cpu and cooler to allow it's fit. Also be sure your motherboard design placement of Memory slots is such that your Memory will clear it. My board's Corsair Vengence Memory JUST cleared it by a couple mm's laterally, and the top of the memory overtakes the bottom edge of cooler by about a quarter inch. If you are in the process of building your system a choice with low profile memory that doesn't have the tall heat spreaders would be a wise choice and safe bet if you are unsure about clearance with a board design that puts the memory slots very close to the CPU and cooler position. In the first photo attached I REVERSED the fan position to PULL the air thru on Left for best clearance instead of PUSHING the air through on the right if you just don't have the room, that flexibility is very handy. I wasn't satisfied with the cooling level and re-positioned the fan on right to PUSH it through later on and it sent the temps down a few more degrees. As you can see though in the second photo, it is much more snug.

Bottom line, a great cooler IF your case and build offers the room to fit it in. I would recommend it for those wanting great overclocking cooling performance and very quiet operation. I think most overclock enthusiasts would be well served to try this value priced solution before expensive and complicated water cooled solutions.
text_fidelity_b: Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO V2 CPU Air Cooler with SickleFlow 120, PWM Fan, Direct Contact Technology, 4 Copper Heat Pipes for AMD Ryzen/Intel LGA1700/1200/1151, Silver/Black

Lexar NM600 M.2 2280 NVMe 480GB Solid-State Drive (LNM600-480RBNA) Modern computers are a lot more reliable than computers from 10 or 20 years ago. Computers are not getting a lot faster every year like they used to. I no longer replace my computer every couple of years. If your computer is getting a little sluggish, instead of replacing the whole thing, you can usually give it a huge performance boost by upgrading just key components. In particular, upgrade your memory and upgrade your hard drive. This SSD does not add a lot of capacity, but it gives you a lot of speed so that programs or databases that you use a lot will load much more quickly.

This drive installed and formatted easily on my Windows 10 desktop computer. It's been running flawlessly since then and the performance is great for me. Performance is great for general-purpose home or business use.

There are a lot of different SSDs on the market these days. Check your computer manufacturer's website to see what is compatible with your motherboard. This SSD has an entry-level design and a budget price to match. High-performance SSDs designed for hard-core gaming or video editing can be twice as fast but also cost twice as much or more for the same capacity.

text_fidelity_a:
WD My Book Live 2TB Personal Cloud Storage NAS Share Files and Photos I just got My Book Live yesterday. I really wanted just a plain old back up, but having an Electronics Engineering degree, I had to stay current. I can't really complain at this point, because I am backing up an 11 year old computer that is slowing to a crawl anyhow. It did not take long to set this drive up on my network. All of my devices immediately found it on the network and play music from the MBL. I had my Kindle HD out in the yard, playing music right off of MBL, while I do my gardening (downloaded the free app for Kindle). It was cool. I feel it will probably be short lived. Last year I bought a cheap WiFi receiver and it was so fast, this year it is so slow. I don't have high expectations from WiFi, and this drive only has the capability to plug into the network. It does not have USB connectivity at all. I do often times want a quick and easy way to transfer files to my new computer, while I do other things. The price was not too bad, but for that money I hope to be able to recover my data even after the WiFi dies. A good back up drive from WD usually last for years. That is what customers are accustomed to anyhow. I will probably update this review in one year. I did password protect my drive before the first file ever got added. I did update the firmware also. So far it is a nice thing to have.
My update on this drive is that it gets better as I use it. I don't know why that new things on my network start out slow and speed up as they are used, but it is working well.
text_fidelity_b: WD My Book Live 2TB Personal Cloud Storage NAS Share Files and Photos

HP ENVY Photo 7155 All-in-One Photo Printer (K7G93A) and XL Ink Cartridges - 4 Colors This is a multi-functional unit. It scans, prints (papers and photos), and does copies. It has two media trays; one can load 8-1/2x11 paper, and photo paper in the second tray. Prints are of very high quality. I printed beautiful pictures and crisp email messages from my laptop in the living room. You can use the same tray for either 5x7 or 4x6 photo papers. I tried to print separately using my personal computer or work computer, they worked well except that this printer did not work with my chromebook. HP gave a message saying that this printer does not support Chromebook. I could not connect wirelessly to my work laptop, only with USB cables. But my personal computer linked wirelessly. The installation is simple, but took an awful lot of time to download HP programs to get the printer going. This printer also supports mobile printing with iPhone, but I did not try that feature. Another feature that I didn’t have in my previous printer is the use of SD card to print quality pictures. The machine has a SD card port and you can insert the card and print effortlessly. The touch screen interface is easy to operate the printer, but first you need to get familiar with it

Other cons are that it does not have built-in fax capability, and does not have Ethernet network interfaces, which may be an additional feature some users may be looking. Such a feature is an ideal choice for printer sharing with your family or the home office or for business. It is a little heavy and an average size printer. I did not sign up for the "HP Instant Ink" program. You have the choice not to sign up if you don’t want it. But if you are planning on this option, make sure that if you sign up and then cancel your subscription anytime, the printer will not get disabled. I have rated this product three stars for overall satisfaction.

text_fidelity_a:
Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red) I really hate to use the word “cute” but there’s no way around it – this is a cute cam! It looks pretty much the same as the original Cube, but offers improved video and the addition of WiFi. Of the new features, the WiFi is the most significant, and makes this far more useful as a cam.

I also have the original Cube and the build quality continues to be very good. These are priced higher than the “no name” action cams, but after using (and breaking) a couple of those, it’s nice to be able to count on the Cube to keep on working. It’s water resistant, which makes it less worrisome when using it in bad weather or around water. It supports up to a 128MB SD card

The form factor and overall design is much the same as the original Cube. It has a magnet in the base that is more than strong enough to keep it well-planted. It’s not strong enough for significant activity (e.g., staying on a bike handle while riding) but it offers the benefit of tripod-like stability without the need for a tripod (providing you have something metal to fasten the magnet).

The biggest change is wifi on the Cube+. I found the setup to be straightforward – basically just download the app and follow the setup steps. I love that the app lets you use it as a live view – that’s a big improvement over the original Cube. It’s a very helpful feature for planning a shot, plus allows me to monitor how things are turning out without having to play the video.

Image quality has been impressive – zero complaints there. I was pleased with the resolution of the original Cube, and this is a bit better. Audio quality is OK. It’s not outstanding, but it clearly picks up voices. I understand that earlier versions of the Cube+ had very poor sound quality, but the one I have (got it in Dec 2015) is fine with regard to sound.

All in all, it’s a great cam with a fun form factor and look. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a small profile action cam with solid build quality and performance. While the price has increased over that of the original Cube, the wifi features are very useful and well implemented, making this version well worth the additional cost.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red)

text_fidelity_a:
Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer Overall, this is a solid charger. The build quality is top-notch, it’s sized so that you don’t have to struggle to put in/take out 26650s, and the 3A charge rate is a treat. However, it has a design issue that, while not a major roadblock, can be quite irritating.

Let’s start with the good news. This is one solidly-built charger. Compared with other chargers in its general price class from Efest and Xtar, this has a lot more heft to it. The sliders are perfect – not too loose; not too tight – and move smoothly without any crunchiness or squeaking. Best of all, it can hold two 26650s without any difficulty getting them in or out of the slots. That’s a great feature since I’ve been using a lot more 26650 mods recently, and getting those fat batteries in or out of some of my Xtar chargers is a major pain.

Other ease of use features include non-slip feet on the base that keep it firmly planted. The included power cord does not have a wall wart on the end – just a regular plug – which is a welcome change. All in all I have absolutely zero complaints about the fit and finish.

Performance is also solid. Each slot is independent, and can be set to charge at up to 3A. However, only one channel can be set at 3A since the total cannot exceed 5A. But even one 3A channel is a great feature if you use large capacity 26650s that can support a 3A input. It cuts the recharge time to the bone. It also has a USB output for charging (2.1A). However, you must leave slot 2 empty if you want the USB charging to take priority. Otherwise, it will charge the cell in slot 2 first, then charge via USB.

The charger has all the customary protection features that you would expect from a good quality charger such as overtime protection, reverse polarity protection, and auto shut off if it runs more than 10 hours. It also has a recovery mode for deeply discharged Li-ion cells. I never use that (if I accidently deeply discharge a cell I no longer use it) but it has the feature should it be of value for your needs. Heat output when running was very low.

The current for each slot can be set to 0.5A, 1A, 2A or 3A. You can also set the cutoff voltage to 1.2v, 3.7v, 4.2v or 4.3v. I use this nearly only with Li-ion cells, so the 4.2v cutoff is what I use for most of my charging. However, it’s nice to have the 3.7v setting for when I want to charge cells for long-term storage.

If you do nothing, the charger will set itself to a 2A current for cells that are greater than 1200mAh, and 0.5A for cells less than 1200mAh. You can override the settings for both current and cutoff independently for each channel.

And that’s where the biggest irritation occurs. The charger has a double row of LED lights that signify current and cutoff levels (plus blink to show operation, and stop blinking when charging is done). Simple and unobtrusive. However, there are no notations on the screen to show what charge rate/cutoff corresponds to each LED. Instead, those numbers are listed on a piece of clear plastic that is stuck on top of the display. It peels off easily and looks like a temporary cover to protect the screen.

In addition to looking poor, the lack of durability of the cover with the numbers listed means it won’t survive for long. Now, there are only four positions for the LEDs so it’s not a huge puzzler to decipher the settings if you use the charger regularly. However, I have several chargers and can go a couple of weeks between using one in particular. It can be hard to remember which LED position means what. And I shouldn’t have to do that – numbers should be imprinted right on the screen and not on a flimsy piece of plastic.

I also don’t care for the fact that the button labels (one for current, one for cutoff) are embossed into the plastic. The black-on-black makes it very hard to see which button is which.

But those issues aside, this is a solid charger that offers up to 3A charging. The build quality and operation are both excellent, and it’s perfectly sized to hold two 26650 cells without a bit of struggle to get them in or out of the slots. The poorly designed screen and button labels drops my score to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up since everything else is well executed.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Nitecore SC2 Superb Charger 3A Quick Charge Bundle with EASTSHINE EB182 Battery Organizer

But of the many many abilities it has, the ability to pull up music, TV, movies and more, some of my favorite things are the simplest. Instant forecasts anywhere in the world, timers and an alarm that you activate merely by speaking to it has really helped me in many ways. Do you want to know the time? Ask Alexa. Do you want to know today's forecast or next week's forecast? Just ask. They are meant to be on 24 hours a day and are activated by voice and so there are no lights on to bother a person when they are sleeping. I put the one in the bedroom not just to operate the television, but more of an alarm clock thing. So if I need to take a nap before my next client, wake me up in one hour. It's that easy. Lying in bed at night and asking what time it is or saying: wake me up at 7 AM. Done. I do not believe this product will replace computers remote controls nor telephones, but I think that it will be a wonderful companion to it, infinite information availability, and who knows what's coming in the future. The upgrades are done on their end so you do not have to buy new units as they upgrade. How cool is that? So far both of these units have worked flawlessly and I have had them for about a month now. Completely unobtrusive, and with plug-in units that are available, you can even run your household lights, appliances and more. I purchased a few of these things and they work perfectly. Kidz Gear Wired Headphones for Kids - Ltd. Edition White Great headphones at a great price. These fit my little man very well, and they are so adjustable even I could put them on to check out the volume.

I'm impressed by the sound quality, especially for this price.

My ONE complaint is that the sound limiter is a separate piece AND this is not clearly marked anywhere on the packaging. I used it for a few weeks before I knew the volume wasn't limited on his precious little ears, it was in an Amazon review that I found out I actually had to retrieve that from the spare part box and use it. I'd thought it was an adapter for other size jacks or soothing. There are no instructions or info booklets in the box, so if you give these as a gift, let the recipient know that volume limiter is separate. Since these are for kids, I don't understand why they don't just limit the volume on the headset itself. Or at the very least, find a way to plug it that holds more tenaciously (like a built-in tie from the headphone to the limiter). That tiny piece is fascinating for kids to remove and easy to lose.
text_fidelity_b: Kidz Gear Wired Headphones for Kids - Ltd. Edition White

text_fidelity_a:
Creative T12 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker System First, I have to say, these sound amazing for their size, picking up even most low frequencies. Crank them up, and they almost vibrate themselves off the table - you can feel the bass just by putting your hand in the open air behind them. I can say confidently that these sound better than the old Boston Acoustics computer speakers that included a small subwoofer.

They are also good looking, have a standard auxiliary input in the back for versatility, and have a headphone output in the front (still trying to figure out when that could come in handy...) They also connect easily to my BB 9700, Xoom, and Win7 PC. Surprisingly, I can even control the volume from the speakers or from the controlling device!

The one speaker has a ~1.5m cable permanently attached that ends in an RCA plug that must be plugged into the other speaker. That can be extended, of course, but somehow, this makes the whole wireless thing less impressive. Somehow, I'd like to have them both pick up Bluetooth separately, but then of course, both would need separate power supplies and receptacles. The point is, for installations such as a home computer setup, what is the point of going Bluetooth for speakers? On the other hand, it is super cool to be able to just spit music from your phone at any time.

My other qualm is that they should have grill covers; I tend to pick them both up with one hand and have to be a bit careful not to stick my finger through the cone.

Overall, I'm impressed with the technology and the product itself. If you have a good use for this particular type of product and can deal without grill covers, I'm sure you'll be happy with the purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Creative T12 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker System

text_fidelity_a:
Misfit Phase Hybrid Wearables Smartwatch - Rose Gold I've been wearing a smaller type fitness tracker for the past 6 months. Just started wearing this Misfit and there's a few things I don't like about it and many things I love about it.
I will start with all that I really enjoy about the Misfit. I like how easy it was to pair with my phone. Even though it sits higher than my other tracker, I like that it looks like an every day stylish watch and not like a fitness tracker. And it's very comfortable to wear. The buttons on the sides are more low keyed and not that obvious that it is a fitness tracker.
Love the sleep tracker of this smartwatch. My other tracker wasn't as good as tracking my sleep.
Step tracking is right on track with what I am walking. Very important to me.
I am still learning all the nice functions that come with this Misfit. So far I love the call notification and the alerts. Like that I can play and pause my music without taking my phone out of my pocket. I am still working on learning how to work my home smart devices using the Misfit but, I know in time, and with practice, I will figure it all out. It's not hard, I've just been really busy with working and haven't had the time with working with all the fun functions.
I also love that I don't have to take it off and protect it if I'm out hiking and get caught in a rain storm. I'm out almost every weekend walking in some nature trail or another. So I get caught in a few unexpected downpours while I'm out.
Now some of the more difficult "to do's" with the Misfit...
Setting the time isn't impossible, just need a lot of patience.
Using a magnifying glass, and good light, helped me get the misfit logo centered in that itty bitty hole at the 6 oclock mark. Whewww...
The watch doesn't have a backlight. So it's so hard to see the time in low light, impossible in the dark.

Canary Pro Indoor Home Security Camera 1080p HD WiFi IP | 24/7 Watch Live Video, Siren, Climate Monitor, Motion Alerts, Two-Way Talk, Night Vision, 10x Zoom, Private Mode, Works with Alexa and More Doesn't live up to the hype. The image quality is not great unless you're right in front of the camera. I placed mine on the tv console, which is on the far side of the room, and has the best views of the living and high traffic areas. You know, where you actually want surveillance...

First unless someone is within 3 feet of the camera, you can't make out faces.

Second the time delay between canary detecting movement and notifying me of activity has been 15 and 30 minutes, including when I've been in the house. When I was out of state, the delay was 15 min. When I was in my own home but in night mode, the delay was 30 min. So I'm not sure how this would be effective in notifying the police because it would give robbers plenty of time to clear out your house before you even see it.

Third you need to be aware of the location you place it and the natural shadows that occur throughout the day. I was getting notifications every 10 minutes. So I changed the sensitivity, but I still get notifications.

I think the concept is great, but the technology has a long way to go.
text_fidelity_b: Canary Pro Indoor Home Security Camera 1080p HD WiFi IP | 24/7 Watch Live Video, Siren, Climate Monitor, Motion Alerts, Two-Way Talk, Night Vision, 10x Zoom, Private Mode, Works with Alexa and More

text_fidelity_a:
Echo (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa, (RED) edition What a disappointment. Bought this for my son for Xmas, and it was a COMPLETE FAILURE.

First of all, this thing takes FOREVER to boot (we're talking like 5 minutes. Not even kidding.). That's insane. It was a complete PITA to set up (kept hanging and needed to be reset and configured again and again), and then, after all that, despite saying it was successfully set up, it NEVER WORKED. Gave nothing but errors.

I'm even pretty tech savvy, and have automated my entire house by myself, so this should have been easy-peasy, right? If this device wasnt a piece of junk, I imagine it would have been.

For example, despite being told it was successfully set up, when I tried to test it by asking it to play a certain song that I often play on other Alexa-enabled devices , it would announce the name of the song and artist, then go, "Sorry. Something went wrong."

Just to be sure it wasn't on Alexa's end or a problem with my Amazon Music premium account, I went to all the other Echos and dots in our house and asked them to play the same song. Each did with ZERO problems.

So I thought, "Maybe it just needs to be updated." So I told Alexa to update, and she responds, "Sorry, I'm not programmed to do that now, but I'm always learning. Try again some other time."

I googled Echo updates and found that Echos are supposed to be auto-updatable as soon as they are connected to wifi, and this one WAS connected to wifi, so this was complete B.S.

I reset the Echo, tried again, it said it successfully set up (again) and, again, it failed to carry out ANY commands. I contacted Amazon Help and waited for a response. I reset, then unplugged, the Echo time after time, waited for 15 minutes, then tried to set it up again. Over and over. Every single time it said the set up was successful. And every single time it failed to do ANYTHING I told it to do.

Worth noting: when I googled the problem, there was site after site and thread after thread of people complaining about the same, or very similar, issues, from as far back as a couple years ago and right up until the day I went through all this. Even Amazon's own Alexa pages came up all over the search.

So, CLEARLY, Amazon is very much aware of these issues and, yet, they still continue to sell these defective Echos anyhow.
text_fidelity_b: Echo (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa, (RED) edition

Linksys N300: Wi-Fi Wireless Router, Linksys Connect, Parental Controls, Home Internet, Wireless Devices up to 300 Mbps Transfer Speed (Black) I've been using a Linksys router for years and it never missed a beat (their wireless G model with the two antennas). But, after upgrading my Internet from DSL to cable, I thought a new router would be in order.

Before buying one I searched for reviews from computer and tech magazines/sites. Talk about confusing! I'd read one review that gave a sterling endorsement for a particular router; then another review from another site that gave the same router a horrible review.

Since my router needs are pretty basic (just use it to share Internet access) I concentrated on ease of install issues. In that regard there was consensus about how easy Linksys is to install. So I went with them again, and selected the 1200 model since it gave me all that I wanted/needed at a good price (but, to hedge my bets, I got it at a warehouse club so I could return it easily).

So happy with this router! Installation was SO simple -- if you can plug in a cable you can install this router. But, should you want to tinker with settings, you can also access the full, detailed configuration menu and tweak settings to your heart's content. I think it took me longer to open up the box and unwrap the router and power cord than it took to actually get it to work.

Performance so far has been excellent. I put it on the ground level of my house and have no problems getting a strong signal in the basement and upper level. I did find that it helps to put the router in the middle of the house rather than against a wall for best signal strength throughout the house.

Considering that my Linksys G is still cranking along after several years, I'm reasonably confident (or at least hopeful) that this will last me an equal length of time.

If you're looking for a solid, easy to install single band router, this is it. Highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Linksys N300: Wi-Fi Wireless Router, Linksys Connect, Parental Controls, Home Internet, Wireless Devices up to 300 Mbps Transfer Speed (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Enjoy...
text_fidelity_b: Kensington Wired SlimBlade Trackball Mouse (K72327U), Black

I plan to keep the telescope 'permanent' through the second-story game room windows. We have a spectacular shot through the preserve. We live on a major migratory flyway. North American bird migrations and including the swarm of Monarch butterflies pass by the windows.

As to astronomical use, the refractor magnification lens system is entry-level. This general refractor-grade telescope serves as the smaller spotting scope on larger reflector telescopes. The scope has standard interfaces to mount better glass and wider angle lenses. It's a great basic platform to expand with higher quality and wider FOV lenses. I have plans to mount a made for purpose high res electronic magnification CCD to capture images. I've already replaced the tripod with a more robust design.

I'm delighted with the telescope as a basic platform for customizing. The main attraction is standard lens interfaces and scalability. The optical enhancements get pricey and will quickly exceed the purchase price.

Easy to assemble, easy to use. A beginner will get the hang of viewing with a little use with progressively smaller apertures as magnification is increased. There are viewing techniques available on YouTubes to investigate.

As expected and fully comparable to other refractor telescopes with a 70mm objective lens and 400mm focal length. Nice value for money.

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included First I like sound! I'm an audiophile at heart but in my life now I'm an audiophile on a BUDGET! These are my first bluetooth speakers. More on that in a minute.

I was looking for on ear bluetooth speakers with a budget of about $50 to $60 and was set on waiting for a sale on the JBL EB45T but then saw these recommended on the wirecutter website (a pretty good review site in my opinion)

There is nothing wrong with these, but nothing really right about them either. They have a nice neutral sound that you can listen to for a long time. For movies and youtube on my computer, they are great. But there is nothing in the sound that is going to wow you either. Trust me if there was something actually wrong with the sound, I'd be telling you. You can listen to these for a long time without ear fatigue. If you are looking for lots of rumble for movies, these probably aren't the right phones for you. But if your movie listening requirements are more modest then these work well for that. For casual background music, podcasts, audiobooks, they will work really well for that.

Isolation is not great. I think the plastic is thin so a certain amount of noise gets in. I wanted to be able to hear a little bit of background noise, things going on in the house, but these push my limit for how much I want to hear. Even though they were open-back my Sennheiser HD-229 did a better job with isolation because of the design of the pad.

Comfort isn't bad and for my ears, the ear cup size is just about right size. I wish the earpieces swiveled a bit more but for my head, they swivel just enough. . They have a left and right and the cups swivel so little that if you have them on the wrong way you will notice.

Bluetooth... These are a pain in the backside on Win 7. When I want to use them I have to go and delete the previous pairing, pair them again and then go to the control panel and set these to be used for output. For movies on the computer, they get out of sync. I even set my movie player (Pot Player which I highly recommend) to use the Bluetooth headphones and they still get out of sync with the audio. I don't know if it's the player, the USB Bluetooth adapter, Windows 7 or some combination of them together.

I like that they can be used with a wire as well as with bluetooth. The controls are a little small, as mentioned by others but I don't have trouble working them.

I also tried the JBL EB45T Bluetooth headphones, which cost almost twice as much, at Target and these sound better overall. The JBL might have had better highs, a little punchier bass but these are more cohesive across the frequency range with nothing tweaked to make them sound 'better'.

Summary: I don't have any other Bluetooth headphones to compare these to but I think most people would be very satisfied with these at this price point for general use. If however, you are looking for audiophile on a budget, it's not here.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black I really like this GPS sports watch so far. Garmin makes a huge range of sports watches. This vivoactive HR is one of their lower priced GPS watches. It doesn't have the more advanced sports training features or build quality of the more expensive Garmin Fenix and Forerunner watches. However, for this price, you do get GPS and smartwatch features in addition to basic fitness tracking.

I tried the GPS mode on a 3-hour bike ride, running my dedicated bicycle computer at the same time. Distance calculations of the 2 units were less than 1 mile different, which I think is very good for small portable units like this. Current speed was always about the same, though looking at the watch to see your speed while riding is kind of difficult, especially compared to the big display on my handlebar-mounted bike computer. You can mount the watch on your bicycle handlebar, but that would of course disable the heart rate tracking feature of the watch. The wrist-based heart rate monitor is not as accurate as a chest-strap heart rate monitor, with a slower response time that is very apparent during interval training (short bursts of high-intensity effort), but you can connect an ANT+ HR monitor to this watch to improve accuracy.

GPS mode has an advertised battery life of 16 hours, which I think is really terrific for a gadget of this size. My 3 hour bike ride burned about 20% of the battery on the vivo, so 16 hours of GPS time is plausible. Garmin also advertises 8 days of battery life with the GPS turned off, but realistically, who buys a $250 GPS watch and never turns on the GPS? Still, I expect to get in at least a couple of long bike rides or several runs before having to recharge this watch. Recharging is very quick using the USB charging cradle included with the watch. Because battery life is so good, you don't need a spare charger for your office like you might need with the Apple smartwatch.

If you have a (free) Garmin account, you can upload your daily activity to the Garmin server so you can review it on their website afterwards. This is useful for tracking your fitness progress (speed, distance, etc) over time.

The smartwatch features are pretty basic (compared to dedicated smartwatches from Apple or Google), showing phone call caller-ID and copying notifications from your smartphone (via Bluetooth) and displaying them on the watch. If you like checking your notifications quickly and don't want to pull your phone out every time it beeps, getting them on your watch is great. If I'm jogging or in a business meeting or at dinner but am expecting an important message, I can just glance at the watch and quickly ignore it if it isn't important. I have my notifications for high-priority emails, SMS, and a couple of messaging apps synced with my phone. This seems to work mostly flawlessly with my Samsung smartphone. Occasionally, the notifications will stop working but restarting my phone fixes that. I don't know if that is a problem with the phone's base software or with the Garmin app that runs on my phone. The Garmin app that runs on your smartphone lets you pick which app's notifications to show on the watch. I do not know how this works with Apple phones. There are some other smartwatch apps like weather forecasts and calendar, but I'm not sure if scrolling through these on your small watch face is really easier than pulling out your phone to view the app on the larger screen there.

If you're comparing this Garmin watch to an Apple smartwatch, yes Apple has a lot more apps, but Garmin has an 8 day battery life compared to less than 1 day for Apple. Personally, battery life is more valuable to me since there are not yet any killer apps for the Apple watch. Having a dead watch because you forgot to charge it the night before is not fun. Also, the Garmin watch has a built-in GPS, while the Apple watch does not. This means you can record a bike ride or run carrying only the watch, not your phone as well.

Garmin also has basic fitness tracking features like resting heart rate, sleep tracking, intensive exercise tracking, step counting, etc. If you're active enough to want to spend money a GPS sports watch (instead of a cheap fitness band), I don't think the step counting is going to be interesting to you. I bike or run at least 10 hours every week of the year and steps have no interest to me. Resting heart rate is an indicator of your health and fitness and I'm looking forward to tracking that. Intensive exercise tracking may also be useful if you tend to slack off during your exercise. Sleep tracking is reportedly not too accurate on this watch (it can't tell if you're really sleeping or reading a book in bed), but that isn't something that greatly interests me.

On the subjective side, this chunky plastic rectangular watch does look like a fitness tracker rather than a real watch. The much better looking Garmin Fenix looks like something you could wear to the office, but this watch maybe not. At least the vivoactive has a very comfortable wristband that should fit well on a range of wrist sizes.

Again, this is one of Garmin's cheaper GPS watches. I think the features and performance are great for this price point, but if you're involved in hard core training program, you should definitely look at the features of some of Garmin's better GPS watches.

I would have given this watch 5 stars for functionality and value for the price if it was better looking, but Garmin seems to have made it intentionally ugly in try to upsell you on their better looking and more expensive Fenix and Forerunner watches.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin vívoactive HR GPS Smart Watch, Regular fit - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sangean H201 Portable AM/FM/Weather Alert Digital Tuning Waterproof Shower Radio White I've tried a few of the low-end shower radios, such as the sub-$10 models from companies such as Conair. The quality of those items is in line with the price tag - yes, it is a radio, but chances it will last about as long as the battery before it breaks.

A friend of mine has the Sony model, which is a big step up in quality and sound. I took a look at that but the form factor was not right. The buttons are on the top, and it is not convenient to use when mounted on the wall (which is where it would work best for my situation). The sound was pretty good, but reception was spotty.

Took a shot on the Sangean, and was really impressed from the get-go. This is one solidly-built radio! Impressive sound -- very clear and well balanced with decent bass. Outstanding reception that clearly pulls in stations that I find hard to get on any other radio in the house.

The design is excellent, with clearly labeled and easy to use buttons. They make a solid click when you push them, and feel like they will last a long time without any problems. Has a large display with backlighting that turns on automatically for about 15 seconds with any button push. It shows the station, time, battery status, and other indicators in large letters (important for a shower radio since I don't have my glasses on in the shower). Has an auto shut off that works in increments of 10 minutes, and a "nap" timer that can be programmed for any amount of time.

It uses 2 D cell batteries that add to the heft, but ensure you won't need to change batteries very often (other reviewers note that the batteries can last for years if used about 15 or so min a day. Haven't owned mine that long so I can't vouch for that yet!)

I mounted mine on the wall using the supplied bracket. It has self adhesive pads so you don't have to drill. They looked like they would be secure, but I opted to attach the bracket to the wall with screws rather than the pads. In addition to security against falls, I wanted to be able to move the radio to another spot down the road without having to deal with the mess of removing adhesive pads. It also comes with a strap so you can hang it on a hook, or hang it from the attached handle (which swivels out of the way if you don't need to use it).

If you're looking for the ultimate in shower radios, this is the only one that should be on your shopping list. Pricy, but worth every penny.

UPDATE: December 4, 2010: It's been nearly 2 years since I started using this (21 months to be exact), and still have 2 of 3 bars of battery strength. Use it about 10 min a day, every day. Still works just as well as day 1. Well worth the price charged.

UPDATE: July 19, 2012: Well, I finally had to replace the batteries. They lasted for THREE years of daily use! Wow! The radio also continues to work perfectly. Zero problems. Given that I never was able to get one of the cheap shower radios to last longer than a year, this has been a great purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Sangean H201 Portable AM/FM/Weather Alert Digital Tuning Waterproof Shower Radio White

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz Delta Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones w/Microphone in Ear Bass All Metal Buds (OldSNM) This is one of those earphones where nearly every piece of praise has to be qualified with “for the price.” But that’s not a bad thing. I like and appreciate high-end earphones but I won’t take a pricey set with me to the gym since there’s a good chance it will get broken or lost. At the same time, I don’t want to listen to the rough sound that the $10 or so buds produce.

This is a great compromise. They sound far better than you would expect give the price but they are no so pricey that it would be a tragedy if they get dropped and mashed by a treadmill (which has happened to me), dropped in the pool (also happened to me) or left behind/stolen (fortunately, not happened to me as of yet).

The build quality is pretty good for the price. The cables are on the thin side, but well-anchored. The 3.5mm plug is angled which makes it easier to plug in, and also keeps it from sticking out too much on an mp3 player. It does not come with a case or any extras other than a set of various sizes of tips.

Comfort is a feature that does not have to be qualified by price – these fit very well and are so lightweight that I don’t even notice that they are on. The set includes a variety of tips to customize the fit to your ear. Since bass response is partially dependent on a good ear fit, you’ll want to experiment with the various sizes of tips to see which offer the best feel and bass response.

The sound clarity is quite good at low to mid volumes. They get rather harsh at louder volumes – these are not earbuds that like to get pushed much beyond a middle of the road volume setting. But while they are in their comfort zone in terms of volume, the sound is clear. The bass response won't shake your skull, but it's decent. Sound isolation is also pretty good.

These won’t thrill you with superlative sound, elegant design or impressive looks, but their performance and build quality are impressive for the price point, and much better than the typical low-end earbuds. Well worth considering if you’re looking for an inexpensive pair of earphones.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz Delta Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones w/Microphone in Ear Bass All Metal Buds (OldSNM)

text_fidelity_a:
Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US) I was able to do a direct comparison between this and the SwissGear SA1908 ScanSmart Backpack. And it turns out that deciding which pack to grab on the way out is surprisingly one of the hardest decisions one could have to make. Both packs are obviously of the best quality with a similar nylon shell, strong stitching, and smooth zippers. Both are designed to fit 17" laptops and have similar interior volumes, and yet the features vary widely. Let's have a look at key points:

-The Targus is perfect for a user carrying a laptop and a tablet and/or Kindle. In front of the laptop compartment is a soft fabric lined pocket to hold a tablet against the laptop and protect the screen from scratches. The very front pocket is also soft with a piece of padding that fits the newest Kindle nicely.

-The SwissGear may be better for carrying just a laptop or two laptops. It has the ScanSmart feature, which is great when TSA allows it to work (sometimes they make you remove your computer anyway, either out of ignorance or their suspicion that you packed incorrectly for it to work - that makes it easier just to remove it sometimes rather than risk a fight with them). And I often store a second laptop in the ScanSmart opening.

-I love that on the Targus, the zipper pulls for the main compartment and the two side compartments can be placed between the bag and your back, thwarting casual thieves. As an extremely paranoid person, this gives extra peace of mind. For that matter, I really like the unique design of these pockets. The side pockets can be really useful, and the big compartment can be accessed from a larger opening. But that uniqueness comes at a cost...

-...and that cost is the looks. I didn't like the looks on the picture, but then it grew on me. In person, I don't really like it that much, but it might be growing on me. I guess the tradeoff is simple: you get a very unique design that works great and you get some serious padding for your electronics and some extra comfortable straps, but that all equals a slightly awkward looking pack. It's not too bad, but I think an accent color would go a long way. In contrast, the SwissGear under observation is quite beautiful and more traditional, yet not as padded or protected.

-The Targus came in a very thin box. It has a semi-rigid pad on the bottom that can fold up to flatten it out or fold down and attach with velcro to add some structure to the main compartment. This is also a very smart feature.

-The SwissGear has a phone/MP3 player holder with earphone exit, for those interested. That's not the best one I've ever seen though, as it is only a hanging cradle for the device.

-The Targus has more padding, while the SwissGear has a better airflow system for your back.

Conclusion: I really love both of these backpacks, and I'm surprised how different two top notch backpacks can be. I can see how the designers have to pick and choose the features they want to incorporate, because you really just can't have it all without making the pack bigger, and I wouldn't want that. They both deserve five stars, absolutely. The Targus strikes me as the pack for someone serious about the transportation and protection of their electronics, or anyone else who is intrigued to try this unique, excellent design.
text_fidelity_b: Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US)

text_fidelity_a: TOMSHOO Portable Folding Windproof Wood Burning Stove Compact Stainless Steel Alcohol Stove Outdoor Camping Hiking Backpacking Picnic BBQ As all Amazon deliveries have been for at least a month, since they dropped the USPS, this one was late.  Unacceptable performance.  This is a great twig stove.  Collapses into a small package and it use it burns hot and clean. Very efficient, leaving virtually no ash or charcoal.  I've had other similar stoves, including an Ohuhu (?) brand.  That one was nicer in one respect, it had no slotted cross pieces which this one has to space the pot above the flames.  In the dark, or when moving and setting up the stove several times a day these little bits could easily be lost.  the other stove had fold-out bits to support the pot. So, nothing to lose, but the folding part was slightly weak and could be broken or mis aligned.  So it's all about equal i suppose.  Anyway, filled with small fuel and started from the top this stove is very efficient and boils water at least as fast as any little gas stove i've used.  The "bio-fuel" system of heating the ignition air really does burn nearly smoke free.  If the stove is smoking you may have over-fed it or have fuel sticking above the hot-air feed holes.  I got at least 400 burns out of my last little SS twig stove and i never took any great care to be nice to it...and eventually wore it out.  If i get 400 burns out of this one i'll be a happy guy.  In short, if you are looking for a twig stove to burn what you find on the trail or around camp give this one a try, you'll probably like it.

We actually ordered this back on June 22, 2013. We still have our TV up on it. We had just bought I think it is 50", TV and needed to put it up above our fireplace mantel. So my husband bought this one and it's been really good. Not one issue with it either. It was very easy to install. Our TV is not flimsy at all and we've had it up there for almost 3 1/2 years. There is full motion range so that you can angle it in a way that bests suits you. We have ours above the fireplace and slightly angled a little downward. I feel like we are in a movie theater sometimes.

The bolts work just as intended. I read a review to be careful with the bolts ( i think somebody didn't know how to read instructions or properly install) We have had no issue and like I mentioned, it's been THREE AND A HALF years and our TV is still mounted perfectly fine to the wall. Now, with that said. If you one to constantly move your TV around, well, then I could see where that might become an issue with the mounting getting loose. My advice. Once mounted, "leave it alone"

Are the instructions easy to read and follow?
Yes, we had no issues understanding and following the instructions.

Can I mount this by myself?
I would probably get someone to help you. It is a little heavy and that is a good thing, you know it's solid.

OVERALL: This TV mount is a good product and we have been very happy with our purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Mount-It! Full Motion TV Wall Mount | Heavy-Duty Dual Arm Articulating TV Bracket for 50 - 70 Inches Screen | VESA Compatible up to 800x450mm | 200 Lbs Capacity

text_fidelity_a:
Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black As a disclaimer, I'm just an ordinary consumer (vs. a technical expert) when it comes to headphones, speakers, or earbuds. Having said that, here's my experience with these in-ear headphones:

As earbuds go, these are not as lightweight as the much cheaper, AmazonBasics and Panasonic ones I have owned. However, it's a weight difference that isn't really a problem, once I get them securely fastened around my ears.

The sound is wonderful. It has much more clarity than the inexpensive earbuds I usually buy. So to some extent the adage, "You get what you pay for," seems to apply here.

These earbuds have a useful extra: they have a microphone built in. Because of that, you can use it to speak on your cellphone, if you'd rather use this than a Bluetooth. Or if you are listening to entertainment media on your cell phone when you get a call, you won't have to unplug this earbud to take the call.

The microphone control has only one button, an on/off toggle switch. There are no volume adjustment buttons.

These earbuds seem to be well constructed. The cord is thicker and sturdier than my low-cost AmazonBasics and Panasonic earbuds.

The piece that fits into your ear has a relatively large casing compared to my other earbuds, but no doubt this is because the technology is more complicated.

These earbuds are an expensive buy for those of us who normally pay $7-12 for earbuds, but if you like to listen to music, it might be worth it.
text_fidelity_b: Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black

So, I purchased this product. When it arrived I plugged it in and transferred all of my iTunes music and videos immediately. I also put Rosetta Stone onto it. There was a constant humming sound but I didn't think much of it - assumed it was just working. I left it plugged in and put the computer on the table. I came back about a week later and tried to access my song files. No go. The computer would no longer even acknowledge that the Seagate FreeAgent was attached. I shut it all down, unplugged the Seagate, waited and then restarted everything...No go. I put the Seagate on a second computer - nothing. I tried a third computer - Nothing. I no longer have access to any of my files. All iTunes downloades are permanently locked away and cannot be accessed. Luckily Rosetta Stone had CDs but as for any other files, they're gone forever.
I tried Seagate and was told to retry what I had already tried which obviously did not work. Basically I paid for a black brick. I would not put any money towards this product or company again. I can't even begin to replace all that was lost.
text_fidelity_b: Seagate FreeAgent Go 320 GB USB 2.0 Portable External Hard Drive ST903203FAA2E1-RK (Black)

The 20 hour battery life is very impressive, plus it can be recharged with a microUSB charger.

The ANC doesn't entirely cover up a screaming 2 year old, but it does a decent enough job. These aren't $200+ Bose headphones actually.

Sounds and music were good and crisp. Bass was lacking a bit. Bass heads won't like these cans.

They're very comfortable. My longest wearing session was 2-1/2 hours. No sweating, no ear numbness. Headphones can sound like heaven, but if they ain't comfortable all is lost. My wife fell asleep with these on for almost 5 hours. NO complaints from her either.

For the money these are some excellent headphones. My one hour flight to Miami was absolute heaven with the ANC on.

Zoom a lot at the same time, and these little batteries aren't going to hack it. In addition, Canon has something wrong (I suspect) with the battery life sensor/indicator. (My guess is the 1.0.2.0 firmware update that's available from Canon is to help that.) On the good side, that's depressed the price of this camera. Since I don't intend to take a lot of videos with this camera, I'm OK with that. :)

I may have also gotten a good one. Over 2 days of playing with it, I've yet to change the battery. It's showing 2/3 charge. It has however, flashed "charge the battery" warnings a
couple of times.

For calibration, this is replacing a Canon A1100IS we bought about 4 years ago as a second camera.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a: SABRENT USB 3.0 Tool Free Enclosure for 2.5” and 3.5” Internal SATA Hard Drives (EC-KSL3) I was all set to return this because it would not recognize my Seagate 4TB SSHD. In disk management it showed up as GPT protective partition. After googling, I found that the only way to get past this was to use Diskpart and Clean the drive--that meant wiping out everything on the drive. Since I had already cloned it, I went ahead and used the Clean command and wiped it out. Still couldn't do anything with the drive in disk management. So using Diskpart again, I used the command, Create Partition Primary. At this point, Diskpart couldn't do anything else. It would not create a volume to format, so I had to use Disk Management to create the volume and format it to exFat. I should state that the drive was recognized by my computer internally when it was connected to a Sata port, but once it was put into the Sabrent, it's drive information was changed and made unusable until I performed the procedure above. Not sure why this happened, maybe because it's a SSHD, but I kinda doubt it since I had no problems with the drive when connected to a Sata Port.

text_fidelity_a:
Neewer 48 Macro LED Ring Flash Bundle with LCD Display Power Control, Adapter Rings and Flash Diffusers for Canon 650D,600D,550D,70D,60D,5D Nikon D5000,D3000,D5100,D3100,D7000,D7100,D800,D800E,D60 While this macro light has some middling quality issues at times, it does offer a viable, and very cost effective alternative to pricier setups.

The light comes with eight lens adapters to cover most of the common applications (49mm, 52mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm). The adapters are plastic rather than metal which gives me some concerns about durability. I would have liked to see metal adapters since other low-price setups offer them instead of plastic.

The flash offers a continuous light setting, or a flash setting to time with your exposure. You can set it to use all 48 LEDs or just half (can select either the right or the left half).

It’s powered by a battery pack that takes 4AA batteries. The battery contacts on mine were initially out of place and would not make proper contact with the batteries. After adjusting the position of the contacts with a screwdriver, things worked fine. The screen includes a battery level indicator so you always know how much juice is left.

You can mount the control head on your camera using the hotshoe, or use it off-camera with an included stand. The stand is really light-duty but reasonably functional.

The control head screen is very easy to read. The controls allow for light output brightness adjustments with a simple plus/minus key system, and mode selection (all/half, flash, stead light). There's also a button to test the light output. The buttons are large and well-labeled as to function.

Note that this unit does not allow for delayed/second curtain synch flash.

It includes four diffusers (white, blue, yellow, clear/semi-translucent) that are easy to attach and remove (twist and lift).

I tested this with a Canon 5D mark II and the Canon L 100mm macro and had zero problems with functionality (other than the battery issue listed above).

This is not pro-quality gear but it’s also not pro-level in terms of price. It’s a great way to play around with macro lighting to see if it’s something you find helpful. The all-plastic design keeps this at the 4 star level, but I would certainly recommend it provided you don’t subject it to a lot of heavy use.

I asked the Cox tech to install it on the gigantic space-gobbling, dust-collecting modem he deposited on my desk, and he said Cox wouldn’t touch anything that wasn’t Cox equipment. Besides, said he, it wouldn’t work with the new equipment, anyway. (This assessment, it develops, was...uhm...in error).

Cox was offering NoMoRobo to its new VoIP customers, and having seen good reviews of that service, I figured it would substitute for the CPR Call Blocker. Because I expected I couldn't figure out how to attach CPR gadgetry to the accursed modem, I donated the now supposedly unusable device.

Mistake.

NoMoRobo turned out to be an endlessly annoying bust. To block a call from a phone number, NoMoRobo has to let the first jangle ring through. This is how it identifies fake phone numbers. Unlike the CPR 5000, it apparently has no preprogrammed numbers; thus every pest's nuisance call just comes right through. And unlike the CPR v5000, it seems unable to identify rogue VoIP/IP rogue diallers, leaving you vulnerable to an expensive scam.

I do technical editing for scientists and mathematicians whose first language is not English. This work requires sustained, close attention. It is not facilitated by constant interruptions. So NoMoRobo's first-ring technology was a deal-killer from the git-go.

Then we have the problem that you can’t signal NoMoRobo that a number is bad with a push of a button. You have to go online to their Website and fill out a freaking form! You have to retrieve the offending number from your phone’s memory, type it into the form, report the caller’s name, say what time the call occurred…all of which adds the insult of time suck to the injury of phone scamming. As hoop-jumps go, it’s brain-banging pointless: the robocallers simply generate new numbers, potentially dialing you from every telephone number in your exchange. Or, for that matter, in any exchange.

With the CPR Call Blocker, if you’re on a cordless extension, you simply press the “Talk” button and then press #2; if you’re at your desk where the device is sitting, you don’t even have to pick up. Just reach over and press that big red “BLOCK” button.

The highly satisfying big red BLOCK button….

Normally I get at least a dozen nuisance robocalls a day, starting at 8 a.m. (or earlier) and running through till 8 or 9 p.m. That's a bare minimum. Yesterday I attached the new CPR unit to the phone system, fairly early in the afternoon. This task, BTW, proved to be *vastly* easier than I imagined it would be. Once the device was online, NOT EVEN ONE MORE NUISANCE CALL got through! Feeling suspicious, I dialed the landline number from my cell phone: it rang right through. That suggests the thing blocked four to six robocalls. Right now it's about 10 the next morning, and so far just one call has managed to get past the CPR device.
text_fidelity_b: CPR V5000 Call Blocker for Landline Phones – Stop All Unwanted Calls at a Touch of a Button - Join Over 1 Million Satisfied Customers

text_fidelity_a:
IDEALROYAL Smart Watch, Fitness Tracker for Android Phones, Smartwatch with Heart Rate,Sleep Monitor,Activity Tracker with IP67 Waterproof Pedometer Watch for Android & iOS for Men Women At time of writing, this is going for $30, but I think it may have been $20 previously. I was surprised to see those prices, because it seems pretty sophisticated. I don't have an Apple watch, but I don't imagine it does much more than this (although I could definitely be wrong). It's a shame that wearing a watch sort of irritates me because I can see a real point to having this, surprisingly.

I think the Apple watch may have wireless charging, whereas this uses a magnetic cable with a USB port on one end. This can be just a little tricky to ensure it's charging while on its side (I guess face down is fine, but then you can't be 100% certain it's actually charging), but you get the hang of it quickly.

You get a surprising amount of information on the small face, and then a few scrolls in whichever direction can give you more information. You get use to that very quickly, too, and it is, in fact, very intuitive. You can always find what you want before too long.

The main face can be flash updated, meaning you can download different themes to the device. There's a couple neat ones, but nothing too exciting. I'm guessing there may be user uploaded versions for the Apple version (or maybe not, as Apple always locks its stuff down too much), and that could happen here, too, but I'm guessing not as many people have this, which will lessen the available "content".

The step count is the main thing, along with the time. The watch usually pops on for you to see it when you raise it to look at it, but not always. Usually a shake will turn it on if it doesn't notice you raise your arm. If nothing else, you can press the button. It's a fine line, because too many false positives would also be annoying.

It seems to last a very long time, like many days. And the battery indicator has five segments instead of the three that some devices have, so you get a better indication of when you'll have to charge it.

I'm not really convinced it's super accurate with my steps, but I'm not sure the Apple version would be either. And then it makes a guess on your calorie burn based on steps, which is just for fun as far as I'm concerned. It can do a bunch of other stuff if you hook it up with your "health" app, but I never bothered setting up that app in the first place.

Other convenience factors include it vibrating when you get a call or text, which can help you notice calls and texts, especially if you have your phone on vibrate all the time like I do (and for that reason miss a lot of calls). You can also read your text messages on here, although not really so well that you wouldn't just pull your phone out of your pocket if you actually want to read it (although knowing if you can ignore it can be helpful). You can also control your music to some degree and tell your camera to take a picture, which will be wonderful if you're one of those people always taking pictures of themselves (of if you just want a picture of you and your friends without having to have someone stay behind to press the button).

It also has a timer. Some of these things require the app to be running on your phone (I'm not saying which ones for sure because I think the manual said the camera shutter wouldn't work without the app, but it does). And there is a "find phone" feature which I can't figure out how to get to work, although I haven't tried much. I mean, it's bluetooth, so if the phone is far away, it won't help you anyway.

The watch and the band look just like the Apple version from what I can tell. The band also comes off easily, so I'm assuming it can be replaced with anything that fits the Apple version, but double-check before you count on it.

Overall, I like it a lot. I'd never consider the Apple version, which I assume costs hundreds, but for a fraction of that, I think it's a pretty cool toy.
text_fidelity_b: IDEALROYAL Smart Watch, Fitness Tracker for Android Phones, Smartwatch with Heart Rate,Sleep Monitor,Activity Tracker with IP67 Waterproof Pedometer Watch for Android & iOS for Men Women
